text.content: Sofia has decided that Cascadia's support workflow will use orchestration rather than choreography — a coordinator will run the specialists rather than letting them talk to each other freely. That decision only names the coordination style. It does not say how the coordinator moves work through the system. Does it run agents in a fixed sequence? In parallel? Route based on the request type? Loop until the answer is good enough? These are different orchestration patterns, and Sofia has to pick one before she can build anything.

text.content: The orchestration pattern determines how work moves through the system, how decisions are made, and where failure points appear. Choosing the right pattern is one of the highest-leverage design decisions a system will encounter: it shapes latency, cost, debuggability, and the shape of every future extension.

text.content: Modern orchestration tools and agent frameworks — n8n, LangGraph, CrewAI and AutoGen — support variations of these core patterns. This lesson walks through the six most common ones, when each fits, and where each starts to strain.

text.content: Chaining is the simplest orchestration pattern. Work moves through a fixed sequence of agents or steps, with each step using the output of the previous one.

text.content: Routing introduces a decision point into the workflow. A router examines the incoming request and chooses the most appropriate agent to handle it.

text.content: A customer submits the question, "Why was I charged twice this month?" The router analyzes the request and determines that it is a billing-related issue, so the request is sent to the Billing Agent. If the question were about a product malfunction, it would be routed to the Technical Agent. General inquiries would be sent to the General Support Agent.

text.content: Iteration allows an agent to improve its own work multiple times before producing a final result.

text.content: A research agent creates an initial plan for investigating a topic. It gathers information from available sources and then passes the findings to an evaluation agent. The evaluation agent checks whether the information is accurate, complete, and relevant. If gaps or quality issues are found, the workflow loops back to the research agent to collect additional information. This cycle continues until the evaluation criteria are met, after which a final report is produced.

text.content: Suppose a research agent is trying to answer a question about a company's recent financial performance. It first generates a search query, retrieves relevant information, and evaluates whether the results provide enough evidence to answer the question. If the information is incomplete or unclear, the agent generates a refined query and repeats the process until it has gathered sufficient information.

text.content: Unlike iteration, which typically repeats a process to progressively refine or improve an output, looping focuses on repeating a sequence of steps until a specific condition is met. In other words, iteration is often used for enhancement through multiple passes, while looping is driven by a stopping criterion such as finding sufficient information, achieving a target confidence level, or satisfying a validation check.
